attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post, not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Faithful in substance. 'or' slightly loosens the original 'and'. The 'speak to their lack of resourcefulness' clause is an inference that can't be measured on its own terms.

contract.note: Reading 'inability' as undependable checking, and allowing tools, fits the context ('reliability is not their strong suit'). The 2024 to Jan 2025 window and the reliability threshold are the evaluator's choices, so interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: 2024 shared task: the best system scored 63% on fact verification with external evidence. That is weak support for the reliability concern. But the score combines verdict and evidence quality on hard real-world claims, not basic checks.

A GPT-4o-based checker won the task, and its authors dispute some reference labels. This counts against complete incapacity and against reading every benchmark miss as a model error. It does not show dependable checking.
METR's qualitative notes show GPT-4o agents submitting unchecked or unsupported answers despite tools. A prompted model also caught all 20 selected errors. Agentic tasks, mixed signal, no rates.
A prompting method improves self-verification and correction on QA, arithmetic and commonsense tasks. It shows partial ability, not dependable checking across basic tasks.

reviews.rationale: The packet has signs of unreliable checking (63% top score, unchecked agent submissions) and signs of real checking ability (InFact, ProCo, METR's 20 caught errors). No item is a representative evaluation of basic fact checking and obvious-error detection with ordinary resources. So neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met, and the resourcefulness inference has no measure.
